faqs.question: Who actually wrote "It's better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all"?
faqs.answer: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, in canto XXVII of In Memoriam A.H.H., published in 1850. It is frequently credited to Shakespeare, and the poem is an elegy for Tennyson's friend Arthur Hallam rather than a love poem.

faqs.question: Is the Winnie-the-Pooh line about saying goodbye being hard actually by A. A. Milne?
faqs.answer: No. A string search of the full 1926 text of Winnie-the-Pooh returns ten instances of "good-bye" and two of "lucky", and that sentence is not among them. It circulates widely under Milne's name with no source anyone has produced.

faqs.question: How do I check a quote myself before I send it?
faqs.answer: Find the work it is credited to in an archive that holds the complete text, then search for the exact wording rather than a paraphrase. If the phrase does not appear in the book it is supposedly from, the attribution is wrong, whatever a hundred quote pages say.

faqs.question: What is the shortest line here that still lands?
faqs.answer: Tagore's "I am restless. I am athirst for far-away things" from The Gardener, 1913, runs to nine words. Dickinson's "Parting is all we know of heaven" is shorter still and works as a caption.

faqs.question: Can I put a famous quote in something I send someone?
faqs.answer: Sending a short attributed excerpt privately is ordinary practice, and works old enough to be in the public domain - everything printed on this page - carry no restriction at all. Song lyrics and recent novels are a different matter, which is why two lines were left out here.

faqs.question: Why do so many quote lists get the author wrong?
faqs.answer: Because they copy each other rather than the books. The same pattern is measurable in academic writing: a 2025 meta-analysis of 32,000 quotations in medical journals found 16.9% did not support the claim attached to them, with no improvement over recent years.

faqs.question: What does "Un seul etre vous manque, et tout est depeuple" mean?
faqs.answer: Literally, one single being is missing from you and everything is emptied of people. It is from Lamartine's "L'Isolement" in Meditations poetiques, 1820, and the smoother English versions in circulation are paraphrases nobody signed.

faqs.question: Should I send a borrowed line or write my own?
faqs.answer: Write your own and let the quote open it. On 214 miss-you pages the median letter is 88 words, so a couplet plus three or four of your own sentences is the normal shape rather than a compromise.

faqs.question: Are any of these lines wrong for a partner in another city?
faqs.answer: Two of them. Barrett Browning's sonnet XXXIII and Tennyson's canto XXVII are both about people who have died, so they read much heavier than a long-distance message intends. The attribution is right; the occasion is not.

faqs.question: Does a quote work better for a friend or for a partner?
faqs.answer: The Dickens line - the pain of parting is nothing to the joy of meeting again - is the most neutral of the ten and suits a friend or a sibling. The two Shakespeare sonnets are unambiguously romantic and will read oddly anywhere else.

faqs.question: How many memories should I put alongside the quote?
faqs.answer: Four or five is typical. Across 214 miss-you pages, 86.4% carry at least one written memory, with 4.5 on average and 12 at most, and a borrowed line does most of its work sitting next to something specific you both remember.

faqs.question: What happens after someone opens a page like this?
faqs.answer: Often they tap back. Recipients have sent 1,434 hug taps across 138 of the 214 pages, and one page collected 512 on its own. That return signal is the one thing a screenshot of a quote cannot produce.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Miss You Quotes With the Source and the Year for Every Line

Miss you quotes are worth sending only when the person credited actually wrote the line. Every line below was checked against the original text — the 1609 Sonnets, the 1820 *Méditations poétiques*, the 1913 *Gardener* — and ten survived while five were cut. That ratio is not unusual: a July 2025 meta-analysis of 32,000 quotations in the medical literature found [16.9% of them did not support the claim they were attached to](https://researchintegrityjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s41073-025-00173-z). The other half of this page is what people send around a quote. On SubhSandesh's 214 miss-you pages the median letter is 88 words and the longest is 1,024, and 43.5% of senders password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% platform-wide. Below: ten verified lines with book and year, the five I cut and why, and what those 214 pages show about length, memories and what the recipient does next.

## What makes a miss you quote verified

A verified quote is one whose wording, author and date you can confirm in a copy of the original work rather than in another quote list. The check is mechanical: open the primary text — here, Project Gutenberg and French Wikisource — search for the exact string, then read the sentences around it to see whether the context still fits.

Context matters as much as wording. Two of the ten lines below are attributed correctly and still get used wrongly, because the speaker is grieving a death rather than missing a lover.

## Ten miss you quotes with the book, the year and the check

Each line was located by string search in a full copy of the work named. Where the text is a translation, the translator and year are given: the English words are theirs.

### 1. Shakespeare, Sonnet 97 (1609)

"How like a winter hath my absence been / From thee, the pleasure of the fleeting year!" Found verbatim in [the Project Gutenberg text of the Sonnets](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1105/pg1105.txt), sonnet 97, lines 1–2. Send it when the gap has run long enough to have a season attached.

### 2. Shakespeare, Sonnet 39 (1609)

"O absence what a torment wouldst thou prove, / Were it not thy sour leisure gave sweet leave, / To entertain the time with thoughts of love." Same edition, sonnet 39. It argues that the separation has a use, which makes it an opener rather than a closer.

### 3. Tennyson, *In Memoriam A.H.H.*, canto XXVII (1850)

"'Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all." Verified in [the Project Gutenberg text of the poem](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/70950/pg70950.txt), where it appears twice — canto XXVII and again, slightly altered, at canto LXXXV. It is regularly credited to Shakespeare. It is Tennyson, about a dead friend.

### 4. Lamartine, "L'Isolement", *Méditations poétiques* (1820)

"Un seul être vous manque, et tout est dépeuplé." The line reads literally as: one single being is missing from you, and everything is emptied of people. Confirmed against [the 1820 first edition on French Wikisource](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9ditations_po%C3%A9tiques_%28%C3%A9d._originale_1820%29/L%E2%80%99Isolement). The smoother English sentence that circulates under Lamartine's name is a paraphrase no translator signed.

### 5. Tagore, *The Gardener*, poem 61 (1913)

"Peace, my heart, let the time for the parting be sweet. / Let it not be a death but completeness." Located in [the Project Gutenberg text of Tagore's own English *Gardener*](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/6686/pg6686.txt), poem 61. Tagore translated himself, so this is an original English text, not someone else's rendering.

### 6. Tagore, *The Gardener*, poem 5 (1913)

"I am restless. I am athirst for far-away things." Same volume, poem 5. It suits anyone missing a place and a person at once.

### 7. Dickinson, "Parting" (*Poems*, Three Series, 1890–1896)

"Parting is all we know of heaven, / And all we need of hell." The version circulating as "all we need to know of hell" adds two words the text does not have. The poem is titled "Parting" and opens "My life closed twice before its close".

### 8. Elizabeth Barrett Browning, *Sonnets from the Portuguese* XXXIII (1850)

"I miss the clear / Fond voices which, being drawn and reconciled / Into the music of Heaven's undefiled, / Call me no longer." Verified in sonnet XXXIII. Read the next line before you send it: "Silence on the bier." She is missing the dead, not a partner in another city.

### 9. Dickens, *Nicholas Nickleby* (1839), chapter 3

"The pain of parting is nothing to the joy of meeting again." Real, and spoken by Nicholas — not narrated by Dickens. He says it while describing a future that never arrives, and bursts into tears two sentences later. Quote it as a character's hope, not an author's verdict.

### 10. Kalidasa, *The Cloud-Messenger*, stanza XLI, trans. Arthur W. Ryder (1912)

"I see thy limbs in graceful-creeping vines, / Thy glances in the eyes of gentle deer." From Arthur W. Ryder's 1912 translation, in *Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works*. The whole poem is an exiled husband begging a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife, which is roughly what a shareable link does now.

## The five quotes I cut, and what was wrong with each

**"How lucky I am to have something that makes saying goodbye so hard."** Credited to A. A. Milne everywhere. It is not in *Winnie-the-Pooh*: [a string search of the 1926 text](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/67098/pg67098.txt) returns ten instances of "good-bye" and two of "lucky", and this sentence is not among them.

**"Goodbyes are only for those who love with their eyes…"** Credited to Rumi. It does not appear in the F. Hadland Davis selection of Rumi's verse (1907) and I could find no Persian original.

**"It is sheer good fortune to miss somebody long before they leave you."** Credited to Toni Morrison and probably from *Sula* (1973), but the novel is in copyright and I had no openly readable copy to check the wording against, so it fails this page's own rule.

**"I miss you a little. A little too much, a little too often…"** This is a song lyric from 1995, still in copyright. Cut for licensing rather than attribution.

**"Absence makes the heart grow fonder."** I could not settle which printed source it first appeared in, and three candidates are in circulation. An unsettled line does not belong on a page whose claim is that the attributions hold.

Five cuts out of fifteen is a third of a small hand-picked sample — not comparable to the 16.9% figure above, but a fair warning about quote lists.

## How long should the message around the quote be?

Short. The median letter on the 214 miss-you pages is 88 words and the longest anyone has written is 1,024, so a quote plus three or four sentences of your own is the normal shape, not a compromise.

That figure comes from 214 pages built since the [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) went live on 28 July 2026. It is two months of data: no seasonal pattern can be read out of it, and it is not a rate for any other occasion.

## What the recipient does after they read it

They tap. Recipients have sent 1,434 "hug" taps across the 214 pages, and 138 of them — 64.5% — received at least one; a single page collected 512. That is the argument for a page over a screenshot: a screenshot cannot be tapped back.

Views are shallower evidence. Those pages have 2,417 recorded views, 11.3 per page and 104 on the most-opened one, but that counts page views and not unique visitors — one person reopening a page twenty times is twenty views, so read it as re-reading, not reach.

## A quote in a text versus a quote on a page

This table compares what the 214 pages actually contain, because those are the parts of a miss-you message that can be measured rather than guessed.

| Element | Share of the 214 pages | Typical count | What it does for a borrowed line |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written memory | 86.4% (185 pages) | 4.5 average, 12 at most | Gives the quote something specific to sit next to |
| "Open when" letter | 92.1% (197 pages) | 3.2 average, 6 at most | Lets one line wait for the day it fits |
| Reunion countdown | 28.0% (60 pages) | one date | Turns "till we meet" into a number |
| Voice note | 13.6% (29 pages) | one recording | Your voice reading the line aloud |
| Password | 43.5% (93 pages) | — | Keeps a borrowed line out of a shared phone |

Memories and "open when" letters are near-universal while countdowns and voice notes are minority choices, so a quote does most of its work beside something concrete you remember. Three fields are missing from the table for a reason: the city, the background music and the "together since" date are pickers that arrive with defaults, so their fill rates say nothing about what a sender chose.

If you would rather send the lines one at a time than build a page, [the catch-a-falling-letter page](https://subhsandesh.in/catch) suits you better: it releases a letter line by line, the natural shape for a message that is mostly a couplet and a sentence.

## When a quote is the wrong thing to send

When the other person wants your words, a quote reads as an evasion, and no amount of sourcing fixes that. A 1609 sonnet sent three weeks into something new is a performance; the 88-word median exists because most people are writing, not curating.

A page is sometimes the wrong container too. If the recipient is grieving, the Browning and Tennyson lines are about the dead and will land harder than you intend. If they are in the same room, say it instead. If they cannot get online, a posted card outlasts a link — [browse the full template set](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) only once a link is the right object at all.

## Sources

- Systematic review and meta-analysis of quotation inaccuracy in medicine, *Research Integrity and Peer Review*, 23 July 2025 — abstract read, full text not retrieved.
- *The Sonnets*, William Shakespeare, Project Gutenberg eBook 1105.
- *In Memoriam*, Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Project Gutenberg eBook 70950.
- *The Gardener*, Rabindranath Tagore, Project Gutenberg eBook 6686.
- *Winnie-the-Pooh*, A. A. Milne (1926), Project Gutenberg eBook 67098 — used as a negative check.
- "L'Isolement", *Méditations poétiques*, Alphonse de Lamartine, 1820 first edition, French Wikisource.

Five further texts were searched and are named above without a link, to stay inside this page's outbound-link budget: Ryder's 1912 Kalidasa, Dickinson's *Poems*, Barrett Browning's *Sonnets from the Portuguese*, *Nicholas Nickleby* and the 1907 Davis selection of Rumi.

failed.item: 3–6 outbound links, all fetched and verified to contain the cited fact
failed.why: Six outbound links, but one was not verified at the URL cited. https://researchintegrityjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s41073-025-00173-z returned HTTP 200 with a bot-challenge interstitial and no article text, so the 16.9% figure was read from the publisher's abstract via the Europe PMC record of the same DOI instead. The other five (four Project Gutenberg plain texts and the fr.wikisource 1820 edition) were fetched in full and each cited line was located by exact string search. Closes when the publisher page serves its abstract to a plain fetch, or when europepmc.org drops below the 3-post domain cap and can be cited directly.

failed.item: No source passes the **swap test** — none could sit unchanged in a different keyword's post in this batch
failed.why: Four of the six sources are Project Gutenberg primary texts, and the Shakespeare Sonnets file (eBook 1105) could sit unchanged in another English miss-you-quotes keyword in this 30-post batch. It is the correct instrument for the line rather than research concentration, but the swap test as written does not distinguish the two, so this is recorded as a failure rather than argued away. Closes only if the verification instrument is exempted the way verify.config.json already exempts dictionaries and corpora.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this query that names the book, the year and an openable text for every line, and the only one that publishes what it threw away and why — which is a genuinely different artifact and the kind of thing an answer engine can cite rather than merely rank. That is not the same as winning the SERP: `miss you quotes` is a contested three-word near-head term where rd.com and BrainyQuote are real authorities, and a low-authority domain is unlikely to take it quickly on the strength of one post. The realistic near-term return is citation in AI answers to attribution questions ("did Milne write that?", "who wrote 'better to have loved and lost'?") and long-tail entry, not position one.

batchMeta.structuralLimitations: CANNIBALISATION. 81 live slugs carry `miss`, and five live English posts already target `miss you quotes` as a secondary keyword (cute-miss-you-messages, heart-touching-miss-you-messages, miss-you-message-for-long-distance, miss-you-messages-for-her, miss-you-message-good-morning). The three closest were fetched from Strapi and read in full: heart-touching-miss-you-messages (1,760 words), miss-you-messages-for-her (1,390) and cute-miss-you-messages (1,737). None of the three contains the string "quote" anywhere in its body, and none prints a single attributed line from a published work — all three are generators of original lines for the reader to send as their own. This post does the opposite: it prints other people's lines with the book, the year and a text the reader can open, and documents the five it discarded. That is a content-type difference, not a tone difference, so the merge recommendation was considered and rejected. The five miss-you-quotes-in-<language> slugs are the language axis and are not duplicates of an English post. BRIEF CLAIMS CHECKED. The SERP supplied in the task prompt was re-run once and came back identical position for position (rd.com, marriage.com, brainyquote.com, pinterest.com, thoughtcatalog.com, adobe.com/express, ibme.utk.edu, goodreads.com x2) — the framing was accurate, not a false claim. The three first-party figures quoted in the prompt (88/1,024 word letters; 43.5% vs 38.5%; 1,434 hug taps across 138 of 214) all match the pinned snapshot byte for byte. QUOTES CUT: five of fifteen — the pseudo-Milne (absent from the 1926 Winnie-the-Pooh text), the pseudo-Rumi (absent from the 1907 Davis selection, no Persian original found), the Toni Morrison line (probably Sula, 1973, but in copyright with no openly readable copy to check against), a 1995 song lyric (copyright, not attribution), and "absence makes the heart grow fonder" (origin unsettled across three candidates). Two further lines survived attribution but needed a context correction in the body: Barrett Browning XXXIII and Tennyson XXVII are both about the dead. SOURCE CONCENTRATION: eleven primary texts were fetched and string-searched, but only six are linked, because the checklist caps outbound links at six; Ryder's 1912 Kalidasa, Dickinson's Poems, Sonnets from the Portuguese, Nicholas Nickleby and the 1907 Rumi selection are named in the body with edition and year but not linked. Four of the six registered sources share gutenberg.org — one post, so inside the 3-post domain cap, but a real concentration. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/europepmc.org, frontiersin.org and journals.plos.org were all at the 3-post cap when capcheck ran, which is why the quotation-inaccuracy paper is cited at the BMC publisher URL rather than at Europe PMC. NOT MEASURED: no claim is made about what the ranking pages target, beyond the one SERP actually run on 2026-09-25.
